questions.prompt: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n items?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — each comparison halves the search space, so at most log₂n steps.
questions.feedbackWrong: Binary search halves the search space each step: O(log n).

mistakes.misconception: Confuses binary search with linear search, which inspects every element.
mistakes.correction: Binary search never scans linearly — it jumps to the midpoint and discards half each time.

mistakes.misconception: Believes direct midpoint access means constant time.
mistakes.correction: One midpoint probe is O(1), but the search repeats halving until found — log₂n probes in the worst case.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm works by repeatedly dividing the list into smaller sublists around a pivot?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — quick sort partitions around a pivot recursively.
questions.feedbackWrong: Partitioning around a pivot is quick sort's defining step.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses the two divide-and-conquer sorts — merge sort also divides.
mistakes.correction: Merge sort divides by halving and recombines by merging; only quick sort partitions around a pivot.

questions.prompt: Complete the trace table for this algorithm when `x = 12`.
questions.codeSnippet:
x = 12
count = 0
while x > 1
  x = x / 2
  count = count + 1
endwhile
print(count)

questions.prompt: A school wants a program to manage room bookings. Explain how decomposition and abstraction would each help in designing this program.

markScheme.text: Decomposition: breaking the problem into smaller sub-problems/modules (e.g. login, search availability, make booking, cancel booking).
Benefit: each module can be developed/tested independently, possibly by different team members, making the system easier to build and maintain.
Abstraction: hiding unnecessary detail and focusing on what is essential — e.g. a room is modelled by number/capacity/availability rather than its physical properties.
Benefit: simpler model that is easier to reason about; implementation details can change without affecting the interface.

questions.prompt: Explain why binary search requires the data to be sorted, and state one situation where linear search would be preferred despite being slower on average.

markScheme.text: Binary search discards half the data based on a comparison with the midpoint — this reasoning is only valid if elements are ordered.
If unsorted, elements larger than the target could be anywhere, so the wrong half may be discarded and the target missed.
Linear preferred when: data is unsorted and sorting cost outweighs search cost / data set is very small / data is in a linked structure without random access.

questions.prompt: What must every correct recursive algorithm include to guarantee it terminates?
options: A base case that stops the recursion, reached by progressively smaller inputs
A loop counter incremented on each call
At least two recursive calls per invocation
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — a base case plus convergence toward it prevents infinite recursion.
questions.feedbackWrong: Recursion terminates when a base case is reached; inputs must progress toward it.

mistakes.misconception: Confuses recursion structure (e.g. tree recursion) with termination requirements.
mistakes.correction: The number of recursive calls affects branching, not termination — a single recursive call without a base case never stops.

questions.prompt: Describe how the bubble sort algorithm orders the list [5, 2, 9, 1] ascending, and state one optimisation that detects an already-sorted list early.

markScheme.text: Repeatedly steps through the list comparing adjacent pairs and swapping them if out of order — e.g. first pass: (5,2)→swap, (5,9) keep, (9,1)→swap giving [2,5,1,9].
After each pass the largest unsorted element has 'bubbled' to its final position.
Passes repeat until a complete pass makes no swaps; list becomes [1,2,5,9].
Optimisation: track whether any swap occurred in a pass — if none, terminate early (or reduce the range each pass since the tail is sorted).

questions.prompt: Define the terms 'abstraction', 'decomposition' and 'algorithmic thinking' as used in computational thinking.

markScheme.text: Abstraction: removing/hiding unnecessary detail to focus on the essential features of a problem.
Decomposition: breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.
Algorithmic thinking: defining a precise sequence of steps/rules that solves the problem for any valid input.

questions.prompt: Which data type is most appropriate for storing a UK postal code such as 'CB2 1TN'?
questions.feedbackCorrect: Correct — postal codes mix letters, digits and spaces; they are text.
questions.feedbackWrong: Postal codes contain letters and spaces — they must be strings.

mistakes.misconception: Sees digits in the code and assumes numeric storage.
mistakes.correction: Codes contain letters and a space, and arithmetic on them is meaningless — they are identifiers, not quantities.

questions.prompt: Two algorithms solve the same problem: one is O(n²), the other O(n log n). Explain what this means in practice as input size grows, referencing a input of one million items.

markScheme.text: O(n²) means time grows proportionally to the square of the input size — doubling n quadruples the time.
O(n log n) grows much more slowly — for n = 1,000,000 the ratio is roughly 10¹² vs 2×10⁷ operations.
Conclusion: the O(n log n) algorithm is feasible at large scale where the quadratic one is not; complexity classes matter more than constant factors as n grows.
